newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian shares resume bull run with record.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian shares resume bull run with record.

text.p: Russia's share market, rested from two weeks of mixed trading, edged highter to record levels, bringing gains on the Russian Trading System (RTS) index to mpre than 50 percent for the year on Monday.

Dealers said competition for shares in a tight market, despite relatively high volumes, would keep prices firm and might send them even higher despite some reluctance by Western investors to buy the market at record levels.
The RTS 24-share index closed at a record 304.90, up from 292.67 at Friday's close and a record 293.33 set during the day on January 24. The index was below 200 at the end of last year.
Over $43 million changed hands, a high volume in this young market.
"There is another series of hysterical buying -- it is not clear whether by Russians or Western investors," said Regent European Securities senior trader Dmitry Starenko.
"Everyone is trying to invest money... liquidity is shot."
Leading shares led the charge, just as in the rally in early January.
Shares were seen testing and sometimes pushing beyond psychological limits on Monday. Rostelekom passed $4.00 for the first time, rising to $4.065 from $3.730 at Friday's close.

Mosenergo utility tested $1.50 and broke through for one trade but ended the day at $1.47, up from $1.46, and national gridholder and utility UES, the share volume leader, tested 20 cents to close at $0.1965 after $0.1820.
Some traders saw Russian operators behind most of the buying but added that Westerners had become net buyers after a couple of weeks of mixed trading.

"I expect this growth to continue," said Pavel Gronbjerg, head of equities trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow, predicting a gradual rise in share prices. "There is no correction looming for this week."
Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said that Russia was still a seller's market.
"Anytime someone buys (a large lot), that has driven the price up," he said. "But we have seen some major sellers that have not pushed prices down. The market has absorbed all the paper (offered)."
Western investors recently have been seen hesitating to invest new money in shares after a three-week, 40 percent rise, chiefly in leading shares at the beginning of the year.
But operators have said that fund managers were re-examing their holdings rather than cutting investment in the market. They said more funds were still to come.
"The flows are still very supportive," said Christopher Granville, director of research at United City Bank in Moscow.
